# Introduction

This quick note is intended to introduce the intuition behind the `NNS.VAR`
function, which serves as a nonparametric vector autoregression.

Install the latest version of `NNS` and the other required packages...

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
require(devtools)
install_github("OVVO-Financial/NNS", ref = "NNS-Beta-Version")
```

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(NNS)
library(vars)
library(forecast)
library(randomForest)
packageVersion("NNS")
```

# `NNS.VAR` Example with 3 Variables: Fed Funds, Real GNP, and Inflation

Using the log differences of each `Real GNP` and `Inflation`, the previous
method creates lowest frequency series. In this illustrative VAR example from
Lutz Kilian[^1], `Fed Funds` (monthly) is averaged over 3-period windows to
align with quarterly GNP data.

The series come from FRED: `FEDFUNDS` (effective federal funds rate, monthly,
percent), `GNPC96` (real gross national product, quarterly) and `GNPDEF` (GNP
implicit price deflator, quarterly). The window, 1954 Q4 to 2007 Q4, is the
archived page's 213 quarters. Its interest rates are reproduced exactly; real
growth and inflation differ slightly because FRED serves the current vintage of
the national accounts.

```{r data}
if (refresh_data) {
  fred_csv <- function(id) {
    x <- read.csv(paste0("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=", id),
                  na.strings = ".")
    data.frame(series = id, date = x[[1]], value = x[[2]])
  }
  fred <- rbind(subset(fred_csv("FEDFUNDS"), date >= "1954-10-01" & date <= "2007-12-01"),
                subset(fred_csv("GNPC96"), date >= "1954-07-01" & date <= "2007-10-01"),
                subset(fred_csv("GNPDEF"), date >= "1954-07-01" & date <= "2007-10-01"))
  write.csv(fred[!is.na(fred$value), ], "data/VAR_example_fred.csv", row.names = FALSE)
}

# Load Variables
fred <- read.csv("data/VAR_example_fred.csv")
series <- function(id) setNames(fred$value[fred$series == id], fred$date[fred$series == id])
FF <- series("FEDFUNDS")
realgnp <- series("GNPC96")
gnpdeflator <- series("GNPDEF")

drgdp <- diff(log(realgnp)) * 100
infl <- diff(log(gnpdeflator)) * 100
irate <- tapply(FF, rep(seq_len(length(FF) / 3), each = 3), mean)

y <- cbind(`Diff Real GDP` = drgdp, `Interest Rate` = irate, Inflation = infl)
quarter <- function(d) paste0(substr(d, 1, 4), " Q", (as.integer(substr(d, 6, 7)) + 2) / 3)
rownames(y) <- quarter(names(drgdp))
head(y)
tail(y)
```

# Forecast 12 Quarters Out-of-Sample Using All Methods

We will withhold 12 quarters of observations as the `test` set. Let's see how
accurate a VAR, a random forest and `NNS` are...

Why a random forest? The Bank of England has recently been posting working
papers utilizing machine learning, specifically random forests:

* [Machine Learning at Central Banks](https://techpolicyinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/Joseph-machine-learning-at-central-banks.pdf)
* [Predicting Bank Distress in the UK with Machine Learning](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/-/media/boe/files/working-paper/2019/predicting-bank-distress-in-the-uk-with-machine-learning.pdf)

Every method is fit and tuned on the training quarters. The tuning steps hold
out the end of the training sample for internal validation; their scores choose
settings and are reported as such. Only the final forecasts meet the test
quarters.

```{r windows}
h <- 12
y_train_VAR <- head(y, nrow(y) - h)
y_test_VAR <- tail(y, h)
span <- function(r) paste(r[1], "to", r[length(r)])
data.frame(Window = c("Training (fit and tune)",
                      "Internal validation: NNS.ARMA.optim, NNS.boost, NNS.stack",
                      "Internal validation: NNS.VAR (pipeline)",
                      "Test (final forecasts only)"),
           Quarters = c(span(rownames(y_train_VAR)),
                        span(tail(rownames(y_train_VAR), 2 * h)),
                        span(tail(rownames(y_train_VAR), 40)),
                        span(rownames(y_test_VAR))),
           Length = c(nrow(y_train_VAR), 2 * h, 40, h))
```

The window of `NNS.VAR` is `max(2 * h, 0.2 * (n - tau))` quarters, 40 here; its
output below confirms it.

# Traditional VAR

```{r var}
# 4 quarterly lags used in VAR
VAR_train <- VAR(y = y_train_VAR, p = 4)
VAR_test <- predict(VAR_train, n.ahead = h)
VAR_fc <- sapply(VAR_test$fcst, function(f) f[, "fcst"])

rmse <- function(f, a) sqrt(mean((f - a)^2))
# A constant forecast path has no rank correlation: NA.
spearman <- function(f, a) if (sd(f) == 0) NA_real_ else cor(f, a, method = "spearman")
test_scores <- function(fc, label) {
  out <- cbind(sapply(1:3, function(i) rmse(fc[, i], y_test_VAR[, i])),
               sapply(1:3, function(i) spearman(fc[, i], y_test_VAR[, i])))
  dimnames(out) <- list(colnames(y), paste(label, c("RMSE", "Spearman")))
  out
}
VAR_results <- test_scores(VAR_fc, "VAR")
knitr::kable(VAR_results, digits = 4,
             caption = paste("Test scores,", span(rownames(y_test_VAR))))
```

The Spearman correlations of the VAR forecasts with the test values are
`r paste(sprintf("%.2f", VAR_results[, 2]), collapse = ", ")` for real growth,
the interest rate and inflation.

This highlights the dual objective of differenced time series data:

* Get the sign right
* Get the magnitude right

`NNS` is able to address this dual objective in its routines as detailed in the
following code chunks.

# `NNS` and Random Forest

## Function to Generate Lagged Variables

The following code is to generate a matrix of lagged variables to be used in
both `NNS` and Random Forest routines.

```{r lag-mtx}
lag.mtx <- function(x, tau) {
  colheads <- NULL
  if (is.null(dim(x)[2])) {
    colheads <- noquote(as.character(deparse(substitute(x))))
    x <- t(t(x))
  }
  j.vectors <- list()
  for (j in 1:ncol(x)) {
    if (is.null(colheads)) {
      colheads <- colnames(x)[j]
      colheads <- noquote(as.character(deparse(substitute(colheads))))
    }
    x.vectors <- list()
    heads <- paste0(colheads, ".tau.")
    heads <- gsub("\"", "", heads)
    for (i in 0:tau) {
      x.vectors[[paste(heads, i, sep = "")]] <- numeric(0L)
      start <- tau - i + 1
      end <- length(x[, j]) - i
      x.vectors[[i + 1]] <- x[start:end, j]
    }
    j.vectors[[j]] <- do.call(cbind, x.vectors)
    colheads <- NULL
  }
  return(as.data.frame(do.call(cbind, j.vectors)))
}

# Test it
set.seed(123)
V1 <- rnorm(10)
V2 <- rnorm(10)
V3 <- rnorm(10)
lag.mtx(cbind(V1 = V1, V2 = V2, V3 = V3), 3)

# Compare to last values of each variable
cbind(V1 = tail(V1), V2 = tail(V2), V3 = tail(V3))
```

# Predictions

## 1 Year Lag $(\tau = 4)$, 3 Year Forecast $(h = 12)$

## Create Forecasted IVs Using `NNS.ARMA()`

Each series is forecast on its own. `NNS.seas` lists candidate periods, and
`NNS.ARMA.optim` chooses among them on the last `2 * h` training quarters.

```{r nns-arma}
nns_uni <- lapply(seq_len(ncol(y_train_VAR)), function(i) {
  variable <- y_train_VAR[, i]
  periods <- NNS.seas(variable, modulo = 4, mod.only = FALSE, plot = FALSE)$periods
  NNS.ARMA.optim(variable, h = h, seasonal.factor = periods,
                 training.set = length(variable) - 2 * h, ncores = 1,
                 print.trace = FALSE, obj.fn = expression(sum((predicted - actual)^2)),
                 objective = "min")
})
nns_IVs <- sapply(nns_uni, `[[`, "results")
colnames(nns_IVs) <- colnames(y)

knitr::kable(data.frame(Periods = sapply(nns_uni, function(b) paste(b$periods, collapse = ", ")),
                        Method = sapply(nns_uni, `[[`, "method"),
                        `Validation RMSE` = sqrt(sapply(nns_uni, `[[`, "obj.fn") / (2 * h)),
                        row.names = colnames(y), check.names = FALSE),
             digits = 4,
             caption = paste("NNS.ARMA.optim internal validation,",
                             span(tail(rownames(y_train_VAR), 2 * h)),
                             "(the selected settings' own score)"))
```

```{r arma-compare}
# Test how accurate the univariate NNS.ARMA forecasts are, against auto ARIMA
arma_fc <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(y_train_VAR)), function(i)
  as.numeric(forecast(auto.arima(y_train_VAR[, i]), h = h)$mean))
NNS.ARMA_results <- test_scores(nns_IVs, "NNS ARMA")
auto.ARMA_results <- test_scores(arma_fc, "Auto ARMA")
knitr::kable(cbind(VAR_results, NNS.ARMA_results, auto.ARMA_results), digits = 4,
             caption = paste("Test scores,", span(rownames(y_test_VAR))))
```

`NA` marks a constant forecast path, which has no rank correlation.

```{r arma-plots, fig.height = 9}
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
for (i in 1:3) {
  plot(1:h, y_test_VAR[, i], type = "l", lwd = 3,
       ylim = range(y[, i]), xlab = "Forecast Period", ylab = colnames(y)[i])
  lines(1:h, nns_IVs[, i], col = "red", lwd = 2)
  lines(1:h, VAR_fc[, i], col = "blue", lwd = 2)
  lines(1:h, arma_fc[, i], col = "brown", lwd = 2)
  legend("topleft", col = c("black", "red", "blue", "brown"),
         legend = c("Actual", "NNS", "VAR", "ARMA"), lty = 1, lwd = c(3, 2, 2, 2))
}
```

The archived page also ran Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests between each forecast path
and the test values. Those treat the 12 forecasts and the 12 outcomes as two
independent samples and compare their spreads, not the forecast errors, so they
are not repeated here.

# Use Forecasted IVs in `NNS` and Random Forest

We will now utilize the forecasted variables in the multi-variate `NNS.reg()`
function. Our first step is to pass these variables through the `NNS.boost()`
function in order to reduce any unnecessary features. The objective function
`obj.fn` and objective `objective` are set explicitly, since this is not a
classification problem.

From there, we use the reduced variable set (if any reduction) in the
`NNS.stack()` function which cross-validates the `n.best` and `threshold`
parameters from the `NNS.reg()` function. Both tune on the last `2 * h` rows of
the lagged training matrix.

```{r nns-stack, fig.height = 9}
# Combine forecasted IVs onto training data.frame, then lag it
new_values <- rbind(y_train_VAR, nns_IVs)
lagged_new_values <- lag.mtx(new_values, tau = 4)
y_train_nns <- head(lagged_new_values, nrow(lagged_new_values) - h)
y_test_nns <- tail(lagged_new_values, h)

# Select tau = 0 as test set DVs
DVs <- which(grepl("tau.0", colnames(y_train_nns)))
nns_est <- rf_est <- list()
stack_validation <- matrix(NA, 3, 2, dimnames = list(colnames(y), c("Multivariate", "Dimension reduction")))

par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
for (i in DVs) {
  index <- which(DVs == i)
  # NNS.boost() is an ensemble method comparable to xgboost, and aids in dimension reduction
  nns_boost_est <- NNS.boost(IVs.train = y_train_nns[, -i], DV.train = y_train_nns[, i],
                             IVs.test = y_test_nns[, -i],
                             obj.fn = expression(sum((predicted - actual)^2)), objective = "min",
                             ts.test = 2 * h, learner.trials = 100, epochs = 100, type = NULL,
                             feature.importance = FALSE, folds = 1, status = FALSE)

  # NNS.stack() cross-validates the parameters of the multivariate NNS.reg()
  # and dimension reduction NNS.reg()
  relevant_vars <- colnames(y_train_nns) %in% names(nns_boost_est$feature.weights)
  nns_stack <- NNS.stack(IVs.train = y_train_nns[, relevant_vars], DV.train = y_train_nns[, i],
                         IVs.test = y_test_nns[, relevant_vars], folds = 1, ts.test = 2 * h,
                         order = "max", obj.fn = expression(sum((predicted - actual)^2)),
                         objective = "min", type = "REG", status = FALSE)
  stack_validation[index, ] <- sqrt(c(nns_stack$OBJfn.reg, nns_stack$OBJfn.dim.red) / (2 * h))

  # Ensemble with univariate estimates
  nns_est[[index]] <- (nns_IVs[, index] + nns_stack$stack) / 2

  # Random Forest
  set.seed(123)
  rf <- randomForest(y_train_nns[, -i], y_train_nns[, i], ntree = 100)
  rf_est[[index]] <- predict(rf, newdata = y_test_nns[, -i])

  # Plot all results
  plot(1:h, y_test_VAR[, index], type = "l", lwd = 3, ylim = range(y[, index]),
       xlab = "Forecast Period", ylab = colnames(y)[index])
  lines(1:h, nns_est[[index]], col = "red", lwd = 2)
  lines(1:h, rf_est[[index]], col = "green", lwd = 2)
  lines(1:h, VAR_fc[, index], col = "blue", lwd = 2)
  legend("topleft", col = c("black", "red", "blue", "green"),
         legend = c("Actual", "NNS", "VAR", "RF"), lty = 1, lwd = c(3, 2, 2, 2))
}
nns_est <- do.call(cbind, nns_est)
rf_est <- do.call(cbind, rf_est)
```

```{r stack-validation}
knitr::kable(stack_validation, digits = 4,
             caption = paste("NNS.stack internal validation RMSE,",
                             span(tail(rownames(y_train_VAR), 2 * h)),
                             "(best tuned value of each component)"))
```

```{r all-results}
ALL_RESULTS <- cbind(VAR_results, NNS.ARMA_results,
                     test_scores(nns_est, "NNS"), test_scores(rf_est, "RF"))
knitr::kable(ALL_RESULTS, digits = 4,
             caption = paste("Test scores,", span(rownames(y_test_VAR))))
```

# `NNS.VAR()`

The `NNS.VAR()` function now accomplishes all of the prior steps in a single
line of code. By default (`naive.weights = TRUE`) its ensemble weights the
univariate and multivariate forecasts equally.

`NNS.VAR` tunes on its own chronological holdout inside the training sample.
With the default `validation = "pipeline"`, the holdout's lagged predictors are
built from each series' forecasts made at the holdout's origin, as they would
be in use, and only observed holdout values are scored.

```{r nns-var}
nns_var_estimates <- NNS.VAR(y_train_VAR, h = 12, tau = 4, ncores = 1, status = FALSE)
nns_var_estimates[c("univariate", "multivariate", "ensemble")]
nns_var_estimates$validation
```

The holdout starts after training quarter
`r nns_var_estimates$validation$origin`
(`r rownames(y_train_VAR)[nns_var_estimates$validation$origin]`) and covers
`r nns_var_estimates$validation$horizon` quarters.

```{r nns-var-scores}
NNS_VAR_results <- rbind(test_scores(as.matrix(nns_var_estimates$univariate), "x"),
                         test_scores(as.matrix(nns_var_estimates$multivariate), "x"),
                         test_scores(as.matrix(nns_var_estimates$ensemble), "x"))
NNS_VAR_results <- data.frame(Forecast = rep(c("univariate", "multivariate", "ensemble"), each = 3),
                              Variable = rep(colnames(y), 3),
                              RMSE = NNS_VAR_results[, 1], Spearman = NNS_VAR_results[, 2])
knitr::kable(NNS_VAR_results, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = paste("NNS.VAR test scores,", span(rownames(y_test_VAR))))
```

# Comparing the Methods

```{r summary}
rmse_table <- cbind(VAR = VAR_results[, 1], `NNS ARMA` = NNS.ARMA_results[, 1],
                    `Auto ARMA` = auto.ARMA_results[, 1],
                    `NNS (boost + stack)` = ALL_RESULTS[, "NNS RMSE"],
                    RF = ALL_RESULTS[, "RF RMSE"],
                    `NNS.VAR ensemble` = NNS_VAR_results$RMSE[NNS_VAR_results$Forecast == "ensemble"])
knitr::kable(rmse_table, digits = 4,
             caption = paste("Test RMSE by method,", span(rownames(y_test_VAR))))
```

These are scores from one forecast origin: 12 quarters for each of three
series. They describe this window.
Ranking the methods would need several forecast origins (rolling or expanding
windows) with the same data, origins, horizon and tuning budget for every
method. The internal validation tables above are the scores each `NNS` step
optimized; they are not estimates of test accuracy.

> **Note (2026).** This page was rebuilt with the current `NNS`. The archived
> page's tables came from an earlier data vintage and `NNS` version and are not
> carried forward. `NNS.ARMA.optim` no longer adds a validation bias shift by
> default (`bias.correction = "none"`), and `NNS.VAR` now validates with
> predictors built from forecasts. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov section is withdrawn
> (see above). See `examples/example-corrections.md`.
